title: How Witchcraft Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and practice of witchcraft, starting with a vivid description of a witch burning at the stake and the persecution of witches in medieval Europe. They trace the shift from neutral folk magic to demonized witchcraft through Augustine, the Cathar heresy and Pope Innocent III, Thomas Aquinas, and the 1484 Malleus Maleficarum. They cover the Salem witch trials and the ergot poisoning theory, regional American folk magic (Appalachian folk magic and Pennsylvania Dutch hex craft/powwow), and the modern Wicca religion founded by Gerald Gardner, including its beliefs, the rule of three, the Great Rite, covens, the Book of Shadows, Sabbats such as Yule and Imbolc, and ritual tools and symbols like the pentacle and broom. They close with Silvia Federici's argument that the witch hunts were tied to the rise of capitalism and control of women. The episode ends with listener mail about a ninja prank and a Japanese phrase correction.

segments.title: Opening and sponsor plug
segments.summary: Hosts open with a note about blogging from Guatemala and a sponsor read for the Camry.

segments.title: Opening scene of a witch burning
segments.summary: Josh asks Chuck to imagine being tied to a pole and burned as a witch, noting hundreds of thousands were killed in Europe and later America.

segments.title: Origins of witchcraft and the shift to demonization
segments.summary: Witchcraft is described as ordinary magic before it became associated with evil. Augustine held that only God could suspend natural laws. Pope Innocent III declared war on the Cathers, and Thomas Aquinas later described demons active on earth.

segments.title: Malleus Maleficarum and the witch hunt handbook
segments.summary: In 1484 two German friars wrote the Malleus Maleficarum, a handbook for finding, trying and executing witches, which targeted women and led to the persecutions.

segments.title: Salem witch trials
segments.summary: Two teenage girls in Salem had convulsions and were said to be bewitched. Accusations, a servant's confession, and executions followed, including Giles Corey who was pressed to death. The General Court's authority was later usurped and the trials ended. Theories include clinical hysteria and ergot poisoning.

segments.title: Regional American folk magic
segments.summary: Appalachian folk magic uses Christian ideas of good and evil and reads nature for omens. Pennsylvania Dutch hex craft, also called powwow, uses symbols for blessings and household protection.

segments.title: Paganism and Wicca's origins
segments.summary: Paganism is defined as non-Abrahamic or pre-Christian religion, often polytheistic. Wicca, about sixty years old, was founded by Gerald Gardner, and is described as the most widely practiced witchcraft today.

segments.title: Wiccan beliefs and misconceptions
segments.summary: Wiccans do not worship the devil and do not believe in the Christian devil or hell. They take an oath to do no harm and follow the rule of three. Their core belief concerns vibrations and channeling energy from deities.

segments.title: Great Rite, covens, and Sabbats
segments.summary: Describes Wiccan initiation levels, covens, and the Great Rite symbolizing union of god and goddess, which may be symbolic or literal by coven agreement. Covers Sabbats such as Yule and Imbolc and Halloween as a time to honor the dead.

segments.title: Wiccan tools, pentacle and Federici's argument
segments.summary: Covers the Book of Shadows, the broom, circle casting, the pentagram and pentacle (upright vs. inverted), and wands. Then reviews Silvia Federici's Caliban and the Witch, linking witch hunts to the rise of capitalism and control of women.

segments.title: Listener mail: ninja prank and Japanese phrase
segments.summary: A listener recounts teenage ninja training that ended with him and friends caught by a family returning home. Another note corrects the Japanese phrase 'puda puda', which the hosts say should be 'pera pera' or 'pera pera' style fluent-speaking term, and a blessing is shared.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts plug the website and the email address and close the episode.
